# Effects of school feeding programmes integrating food systems components on health, nutrition, education and food systems outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review protocol

**Authors:** Sachin Shinde; Ali Aanish Rehman; Cinta Nurindah Sari; Wafaie Fawzi

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Global Health and Population, Harvard T H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Harvard Kennedy School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Global Health and Social Medicine, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

School feeding programmes reach over 466 million children globally, making them one of the largest social safety nets worldwide. Beyond providing immediate nutritional benefits, school feeding programmes increasingly aim to strengthen local food systems through procurement from smallholder farmers, support for sustainable agriculture, community kitchen involvement and broader development outcomes. However, evidence on how school feeding programmes can simultaneously improve nutrition and educational outcomes while transforming food systems in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains fragmented. This systematic review will synthesise evidence on the effects of school feeding interventions with explicit food system components on health, nutrition, education and food system outcomes among school-age children and adolescents in LMICs.

We conducted comprehensive searches in MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase (Ovid), CENTRAL (Cochrane Library), Web of Science, Google Scholar, completed on 18 February 2026, with grey literature searches ongoing and to be completed subsequently. We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs), non-RCTs and quasi-experimental studies with comparison groups examining school feeding interventions with food system components among school-age children and adolescents (5–19 years) in LMICs. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, review full texts, extract data and assess study quality using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tools (RoB 2 for RCTs and Risk Of Bias In Non-Randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) for non-randomised studies). Certainty of evidence will be assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. We will conduct narrative synthesis using the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines and meta-analysis where appropriate.

Ethical approval is not required for this systematic review as no primary data will be collected. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentations and policy briefs targeting international organisations, governments and development partners working on school feeding and food systems in LMICs.

Registration: Open Science Framework https://osf.io/p83tb/

- Comprehensive search: five major databases plus structured grey literature search to capture both peer-reviewed and non-indexed programme evaluations.

- Rigorous eligibility criteria: prespecified four-criterion framework with dual independent review and audit trail to ensure consistent classification and reduce selection bias.

- Inclusive study designs: inclusion of randomised controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies, assessed using Risk Of Bias In Non-Randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) for transparent appraisal of heterogeneous evidence.

- Broad outcome scope: coverage of health, education, food systems and implementation outcomes to enable cross-Sustainable Development Goals synthesis.

- Key evidence limitations: restricting to explicitly described food system components may exclude relevant HGSF-like programmes, while food system outcomes are often inconsistently defined and likely to yield low-certainty evidence ratings.

## Background

School feeding programmes represent one of the world’s largest and most widespread social safety net interventions, reaching over 466 million children across 161 countries.1 In 2020, approximately 310 million children benefited from school meals in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), representing about 40% of school-age children in these contexts.2 These programmes are implemented at a global cost of approximately US$84 billion annually, with governments bearing most of this expenditure.1

School feeding programmes traditionally focus on addressing immediate hunger, improving nutritional status and enhancing educational access and performance. A recent meta-analysis showed school feeding programmes increased school attendance (effect size 0.12–0.13 SD), enrolment (0.13 SD) and improved learning outcomes (0.08–0.15 SD),3 while also contributing to improved nutritional outcomes including reduced stunting, underweight and micronutrient deficiencies among beneficiaries.4

Over the past two decades, there has been growing recognition that school feeding programmes can serve broader development objectives beyond direct benefits to children.5 The concept of ‘home-grown school feeding’ (HGSF) emerged as an approach that explicitly links school feeding to local agricultural development, procurement from smallholder farmers and strengthening of local food value chains.6 This approach aims to create a ‘triple win’: improving child nutrition and education, providing stable markets and income for smallholder farmers and catalysing broader food systems transformation.

The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has reinforced this integrated perspective, with school feeding programmes positioned to contribute to multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) including zero hunger (SDG 2), quality education (SDG 4), decent work and economic growth (SDG 8) and sustainable consumption and production (SDG 12).7 8 International frameworks such as the UN Food Systems Summit and the UN Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016–2025) emphasise the need for food systems approaches that address nutrition, livelihoods, sustainability and equity simultaneously.9

Although substantial evidence documents the nutritional and educational benefits of school feeding programmes, important gaps remain in understanding their broader food systems impacts.10 11 In particular, there is limited synthesis of evidence on interventions that explicitly integrate food systems components—defined here as programmatic elements that deliberately link school meal procurement to local agricultural production and value chains, including local food procurement, farmer engagement and value chain strengthening.12 The influence of programme design features, including procurement modalities, menu planning and farmer support mechanisms, on outcomes across nutrition, education and food system domains remains insufficiently understood.11

Moreover, few studies comprehensively assess effects on farmer livelihoods, agricultural practices and local food value chains.13 14 Evidence is also scarce on implementation processes, costs and the sustainability of integrated school feeding food systems approaches, as operational challenges and logistical barriers are commonly reported but not rigorously quantified.11 In addition, the role of contextual factors, such as agricultural potential, market infrastructure and institutional capacity, in shaping programme effectiveness, has not been adequately examined.14 There is also minimal analysis of potential unintended consequences or trade-offs between nutritional, educational and food system objectives.15 Finally, existing systematic reviews have predominantly focused on nutrition and education outcomes, with limited comprehensive assessment of food systems outcomes and implementation factors in HGSF programmes.3 4 10 Unlike Drake et al,10 who synthesised effects of school meal provision on nutrition and education outcomes using RCTs and controlled before–after studies, the present review requires explicit food system components, extends outcomes to farmer livelihoods, value chains, cost-effectiveness and equity, and includes a broader range of quasi-experimental designs with a search updated through February 2026.

This systematic review is timely given growing policy interest in school feeding programmes that simultaneously pursue nutrition, education and food system goals. As governments and development partners invest in integrated approaches, evidence remains fragmented across disciplines and contexts, underscoring the need for a systematic synthesis to consolidate what is known and clarify how food system-oriented school feeding interventions affect outcomes across sectors.

The review will also generate practical insights on effective implementation, cost-effectiveness and contextual drivers of success, supporting more efficient use of public resources. Given the scale of investment in school feeding, its relevance to multiple SDGs, and the need to rebuild resilient programmes following COVID-19-related disruptions, robust evidence on integrated approaches is both timely and critical.

## Objectives

### Main objective

To systematically review and synthesise evidence on the effects of school feeding interventions with food system components on health, nutrition, education and food systems outcomes among school-age children (5–19 years) in low and middle-income countries.

### Specific objectives

- To describe the characteristics of school feeding interventions with food systems components, including programme design features, implementation approaches, target populations and contexts.

- To assess the effects of these interventions on the health, nutrition, educational outcomes of school-age children, food systems outcomes and other relevant outcomes.

- To identify factors that influence intervention effectiveness, including programme design features, implementation quality, context characteristics and cost-effectiveness.

- To examine equity considerations and differential effects across gender, socioeconomic status, geographic context and farmer characteristics.

- To identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research.

## Methods

This protocol follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines.16 The completed systematic review will follow PRISMA reporting guidelines17 and the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines.18 The review is planned to be conducted between January 2026 and November 2026, with database searches completed on 18 February 2026 and screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and synthesis to be completed by the end date.

### Eligibility criteria

The inclusion and exclusion criteria are outlined below and summarised in Population, Intervention, Control, Outcome and Study Design (PICOS) format in table 1.

*Table 1 Eligibility criteria in PICOS format*

| Component | Criteria |
|---|---|
| Population | School-age children (5–19 years) in primary or secondary schools in LMICs |
| Intervention | School feeding (meals or take-home rations) plus at least one food system component: local procurement, farmer engagement/support, value chain development or integrated agricultural development |
| Comparison | No intervention, school feeding without food system components, alternative models or other interventions |
| Outcomes | Primary: nutrition (anthropometry, micronutrient status, dietary diversity); education (enrolment, attendance, completion, learning); and health (cognitive function, socio-emotional and psychological well-being, depression, anxiety, psychosocial mediators such as hunger and food insecurity)Secondary: food systems outcomes (farm income, production, market access, value chains), household food security, gender, costs, sustainability |
| Study design | RCTs, non-RCTs, quasi-experimental studies with comparison groups (controlled before–after, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, propensity score matching, instrumental variables) |

#### Inclusion criteria

- We will include experimental and quasi-experimental studies with comparison groups evaluating school feeding interventions that incorporate food system components. Eligible designs include randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including individual, cluster, stepped-wedge, factorial (with at least one relevant intervention arm) and crossover designs with appropriate washout periods. Non-RCTs and quasi-experimental designs with comparison groups will also be included, such as controlled before–after studies, difference-in-differences analyses, regression discontinuity designs, interrupted time series with a control group, propensity score matching studies, instrumental variable approaches and synthetic control methods.

- Studies must include a concurrent or historical comparison group, report baseline and endline measurements (or multiple time points for interrupted time series designs), present quantitative outcome data, account for baseline differences in non-randomised analyses and provide sufficient methodological detail to allow assessment of study quality and risk of bias.

- The primary population of interest includes school-age children and adolescents aged 5–19 years enrolled in primary or secondary education in formal school settings. Studies may also include additional participants relevant to food systems outcomes, such as farmers and farmer organisations supplying school feeding programmes, value chain actors, school food service personnel, households of enrolled children and community members involved in programme implementation.

- Eligible studies must be conducted in LMICs, as defined by the World Bank country classification applicable at the time of study implementation.19 Educational settings may include public, private, community or faith-based schools across urban, peri-urban and rural contexts, including fragile and conflict-affected settings outside the acute emergency phase.

- All included interventions must involve school-based food provision, including in-school meals, take-home rations or combined approaches, delivered for a minimum of one school term. In addition, interventions must explicitly include at least one food system component, such as local farming support, procurement policies or practices, farmer engagement and support, value chain development activities or integrated approaches linking school feeding with agricultural development.

- Eligible studies may compare school feeding interventions with food system components to no intervention or wait-list controls, to standard school feeding without food system components or to alternative intervention models. Comparisons across different designs, intensities or durations of food systems integration will also be included.

- Studies must report at least one outcome of interest. Eligible outcomes include health, nutritional and educational outcomes among children as well as food systems outcomes at the farmer, value chain or system level. Additional outcomes may include household, gender, cost and economic, environmental sustainability, implementation and unintended outcomes, measured at baseline, during implementation, postintervention or follow-up.

- No language restrictions will be applied. We will include peer-reviewed journal articles and grey literature, including reports from international organisations, governments and research institutions with sufficient methodological detail.

### Decision rules for classifying the food system components

A study will be judged to include a food system component only if the intervention description explicitly names at least one of the following four activities that link the school feeding programme to local agricultural or food supply systems: (1) local or regional procurement of food commodities from smallholder farmers, producer organisations, cooperatives or domestic suppliers (as distinct from imported, donated or unspecified commercial supply); (2) direct engagement with or targeted support to farmers supplying the programme, including training, inputs, credit or aggregation support; (3) value-chain development activities that connect producers, processors, transporters or storage facilities to the school feeding supply, including quality assurance or market-linkage mechanisms or (4) integrated programming in which agricultural or rural development is an explicit cco-objective of the school feeding intervention. Studies describing only food provision, menu composition or donor-funded commodity distribution without any of criteria (1)–(4) above will be excluded. Where the presence of a qualifying component is ambiguous, two reviewers will classify the study independently using the primary study report together with any linked programme or implementation documentation, and disagreements will be resolved by discussion with a third reviewer. Classification decisions and supporting text will be recorded in the data extraction form to allow audit and replication.

#### Exclusion criteria

Studies will be excluded if they:

- Do not include school-age children or adolescents aged 5–19 years as participants.

- Are conducted exclusively in high-income countries.

- Do not include a school feeding component.

- Do not include any explicit food system components, such as farming, local procurement, farmer engagement, preparation (cooking and processing), distribution, value chain development or waste management.

- Are implemented exclusively in acute emergency or humanitarian settings without a development or recovery focus.

- Employ study designs without a comparison group or baseline measurements, including uncontrolled before–after or cross-sectional designs.

- Report no quantitative outcomes of interest.

- Are purely qualitative studies without quantitative outcome data.

- Are simulation or modelling studies, economic analyses without effectiveness data, editorials, commentaries, reviews, dissertations, theses or study protocols without results.

- Are duplicate publications reporting the same data (in such cases, the most complete report will be included).

### Information sources and search strategy

This systematic review drew on a focused search strategy to capture evidence on school feeding interventions with food system components. Given the multisectoral nature of these interventions, spanning health, nutrition, education, agriculture, economics and social sciences, we searched major bibliographic databases to ensure comprehensive coverage of peer-reviewed literature.

Systematic searches were conducted in MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (via Ovid), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Web of Science Core Collection. Grey literature searches will subsequently be conducted using Google Scholar. Database searches were completed on 18 February 2026. Searches were tailored to each database using a combination of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to school feeding, food system, nutrition, education and low and middle-income country settings. For Google Scholar, the first 50 results for each search string will be screened to identify relevant studies, adapting the PubMed strategy.

The search strategy focused on four broad, inter-related concepts to ensure comprehensive identification of relevant studies. The first concept is the population, encompassing children and adolescents enrolled in primary and secondary schools, who are the primary beneficiaries of school feeding interventions. The second concept is the intervention itself, including all forms of school feeding programmes such as in-school meals, snacks, take-home rations and other nutrition-focused initiatives delivered within educational settings. The third concept pertains to food system components, with particular attention to local procurement, HGSF, smallholder farmer engagement and value chain linkages that connect agricultural production to school feeding programmes. The fourth concept is the contextual setting, focusing on LMICs, reflecting the geographical and socioeconomic environments where these interventions are often implemented.

These four concepts were combined using Boolean operators, and search terms were adapted for each database using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms to optimise both sensitivity and specificity, ensuring that the strategy captured the full breadth of relevant evidence across multiple disciplines. The detailed PubMed search strategy is provided in online supplementary table 1 and was further adapted for other databases to account for differences in syntax, controlled vocabulary and indexing. No study design filter was applied to the database searches to maximise sensitivity and ensure that all potentially eligible studies, including those using non-standard terminology for quasi-experimental designs, were captured at the screening stage.

To minimise publication bias and capture evidence not indexed in bibliographic databases, we will conduct a structured grey literature search focusing on programme evaluations, impact assessments and country case studies of school feeding in LMICs. We will systematically search the institutional repositories and online databases of key international organisations, including World Food Programme, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, United Nations Children’s Fund, World Bank Open Knowledge Repository and Global Child Nutrition Foundation as well as regional development banks such as African Development Bank, Inter-American Development Bank and Asian Development Bank, and relevant bilateral agencies (eg, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit). We will review national school feeding policy documents and programme reports from the 10 LMICs with the largest programmes, as identified in the State of School Feeding Worldwide 2024,1 and search the websites of key research initiatives, including Partnership for Child Development, HGSF Global Programme and Feed the Future.

Grey literature search will use simplified keyword combinations derived from the main strategy (eg, ‘school feeding’, ‘school meals’, ‘home-grown school feeding’, ‘local procurement’ and ‘food systems’) and all relevant reports, evaluations, working papers and policy briefs published from 2000 onward will be screened. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews will be hand-searched, and all eligible records will be imported into Covidence and screened using the same criteria applied to database results.

All updates will be documented, including dates and numbers of new records identified. Detailed search strategies for each database and supplementary sources are provided as supplementary materials. If substantial new evidence emerges after analysis, findings and conclusions will be revised accordingly.

### Study selection and screening

The study selection process will follow three main stages: deduplication of search results, title and abstract screening and full-text screening. All stages will be conducted independently by two reviewers using standardised, pilot-tested forms with prespecified eligibility criteria. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.

All citations will be managed using EndNote (X9 or later) for initial storage and deduplication, followed by export to Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for blinded independent screening, conflict resolution and documentation of screening progress. Duplicate records will be identified through automated and manual review at both EndNote and Covidence stages, with quality checks performed on random samples.

Title and abstract screening will be conducted using a structured, pilot-tested form based on eligibility criteria including population, setting, intervention, study design and outcomes of interest. A liberal inclusion threshold will be applied: citations will proceed to full-text review if either reviewer indicates potential eligibility.

Full-text screening will use a detailed eligibility assessment form covering population, intervention, comparison, outcomes, study design and language/publication criteria. Two reviewers will independently assess all full texts, resolving disagreements through discussion or third reviewer arbitration. Authors will be contacted for clarification where eligibility is unclear, with up to two contact attempts. Studies with multiple reports will be linked, and data will be extracted from all relevant publications to create a comprehensive dataset. Non-English studies will be included if translation can be obtained and verified. Where translation is required, studies will be translated by a team member or professional translator with fluency in the relevant language. The study selection process will be documented using a PRISMA-P flow diagram,16 detailing records identified, duplicates removed, screening and eligibility assessments, exclusions with reasons and studies included in qualitative and quantitative syntheses.

### Data extraction

Data will be independently extracted by two reviewers using standardised, pilot-tested forms in Covidence, capturing all relevant information on study characteristics, participants, interventions, outcomes and results. The data extraction form will be developed based on the conceptual framework, eligibility criteria, outcomes of interest, potential effect modifiers and guidance from Cochrane templates and previous systematic reviews. The form will be piloted on a diverse set of studies and refined iteratively to ensure clarity, completeness and consistency. Calibration exercises will be conducted to harmonise extraction between reviewers prior to full-scale data collection. Inter-rater agreement will be assessed after each calibration exercise, with a minimum agreement threshold of 80% required before reviewers proceed to independent full-scale screening and data extraction.

The extraction process will capture general study information (authors, year, publication type, country, funding, conflicts of interest), study design and methodology (including randomisation, theoretical framework, study dates and setting), participant characteristics (school and student-level details, nutritional, educational, socioeconomic and food security indicators) and intervention characteristics. For school feeding programmes, details on feeding modalities, menu composition, feeding schedule, food quality and programme implementation will be collected. Food system components, including local procurement practices, farmer engagement, value chain development and integrated programming will also be systematically extracted. Implementation arrangements, staffing, monitoring systems, costs and fidelity measures will be documented, along with characteristics of comparison or control conditions.

Outcome-level data will be extracted for all relevant domains, including health, nutrition, education, food system, household, gender, costs, environment and implementation. Information will include definitions, measurement tools, time points, sample sizes, summary statistics, effect sizes, adjusted analyses, clustering, subgroup analyses and adverse or unintended outcomes. Multiple reports of the same study will be linked, with the most complete report serving as the primary source and unique data extracted from all reports. Missing data will be noted, and study authors will be contacted for clarification or additional information where needed.

Discrepancies between reviewers will be reconciled through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer, and quality checks will be performed on a random subset of extractions. All data manipulations, resolutions and updates will be documented to ensure transparency, reproducibility and compliance with data sharing and retention policies.

### Assessment of risk of bias and study quality

Risk of bias will be assessed independently by two reviewers for all included studies, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. RCTs will be evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool,20 including the cluster-RCT variant when appropriate.21 Assessments will consider bias arising from the randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcomes and selection of the reported result. For school feeding interventions, lack of participant or personnel blinding will not automatically indicate high risk but will be considered in the context of outcome type (objective vs subjective).

Non-randomised studies will be assessed using the Risk Of Bias In Non-Randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool,22 covering bias due to confounding, selection of participants, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement and selection of reported results. Critical confounders include baseline nutritional status, socioeconomic indicators, school characteristics, local agricultural capacity, educational measures and community food security.

Certainty of evidence for each outcome will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.23 Evidence from randomised trials will start at high certainty and non-randomised studies at low certainty, with potential downgrading for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or publication bias, and potential upgrading for large effects, dose–response relationships or plausible confounding. Findings will be summarised in GRADE tables, including effect estimates, certainty ratings and plain-language summaries.

### Data synthesis and analysis

Given the expected heterogeneity in interventions, study designs, contexts and outcome measures, we will adopt a mixed synthesis approach, combining narrative and quantitative methods. Narrative synthesis will be conducted for all included studies using the SWiM guidelines,18 providing structured summaries of study characteristics, intervention features, population, outcomes, effects and risk of bias. We will explore relationships between intervention components, context, implementation and outcomes and examine patterns of heterogeneity qualitatively, using structured tables, effect direction plots, box plots and vote counting to visualise findings where meta-analysis is not feasible.

Quantitative synthesis will be undertaken where appropriate, defined by sufficient homogeneity across populations, interventions, comparisons and outcome measures, with at least three studies reporting the same outcome. Priority outcomes for quantitative synthesis will include undernutrition prevalence, anaemia prevalence, school attendance or enrolment rates and farm income or agricultural productivity, reflecting the core nutrition, education and food system domains of this review. Continuous outcomes will be expressed as standardised mean differences or mean differences, and dichotomous outcomes as risk ratios, ORs or risk differences.

Cluster-randomised trials will account for clustering via reported intraclass correlations or external estimates, and multiarm or multi-time-point studies will be appropriately managed to avoid unit-of-analysis errors. Random-effects meta-analysis will be the primary model, with fixed-effect models used for sensitivity analyses. Heterogeneity will be assessed using visual inspection, χ2 tests, I², τ² and prediction intervals, with subgroup analyses and meta-regression conducted to explore sources of variability by intervention, population, context and study characteristics (eg, by age group, by type of food system component, by country income level). Heterogeneity will be interpreted in context rather than by fixed thresholds; however, as a general guide, I² values above 75% combined with a wide prediction interval spanning both appreciable benefit and harm will prompt us to consider whether pooling remains meaningful, with a decision to abandon meta-analysis made jointly with narrative synthesis of clinical and methodological diversity across included studies. Small-study effects and publication bias will be assessed for meta-analyses including ≥10 studies, using funnel plots. Evidence of bias will inform GRADE certainty assessments and interpretation.23

Data management and analysis will employ EndNote, Covidence, Stata and Excel, with robust quality control procedures including independent duplicate extraction, double data entry, verification of calculations, risk of bias assessment and code review. Missing study, outcome or publication-level data will be addressed by contacting authors. All procedures, decisions and deviations will be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

### Registration and reporting

This systematic review protocol has been registered on the Open Science Framework database (ID https://osf.io/p83tb/). In the event of protocol amendments, the date of each amendment will be accompanied by a description of each change and the rationale on Open Science Framework. This protocol was written in accordance with the PRISMA-P guidelines.16 We will report the completed systematic review following the SWiM guideline18 and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.21 A completed PRISMA-P checklist is provided as online supplementary file 1.

## Discussion

This systematic review is expected to make several important contributions. First, it will comprehensively synthesise evidence from interventions that explicitly integrate food system components, assessing their effects across nutrition, education and food system domains. By examining conceptual frameworks and causal pathways, the review will clarify mechanisms through which school feeding influences food systems outcomes, from local procurement and farmer support to broader market development. It will identify effective programme designs, implementation strategies and contextual factors that contribute to success, and assess multisectoral integration across nutrition, education, agriculture and rural development. Additionally, the review will explore equity implications, highlighting differential effects across population subgroups and identify critical evidence gaps and research priorities to guide future studies.

The findings will have direct implications for policy and practice. Evidence on programme features associated with positive outcomes will inform programme design and delivery, while insights into local procurement strategies and food system integration will support national policy development. Cost-effectiveness evidence will guide resource allocation and investment decisions, and lessons on multisectoral coordination will aid collaboration across education, nutrition, agriculture and social protection sectors. The review will also identify appropriate monitoring and evaluation indicators, informing robust evaluation frameworks for school feeding initiatives.

We anticipate several challenges. Heterogeneity in interventions and study designs may limit opportunities for meta-analysis, and variations in outcome measurement, particularly for food system indicators, may complicate synthesis. Many studies employ quasi-experimental designs, requiring careful risk of bias assessment, and selective reporting of positive results may bias conclusions. Context-dependent effects may limit generalisability. These challenges will be addressed through comprehensive search strategies, inclusion of diverse study designs, structured narrative synthesis, subgroup analyses and GRADE-based assessment of certainty of evidence.

In conclusion, this review will provide a rigorous, evidence-based understanding of how school feeding programmes can simultaneously improve child nutrition and education while strengthening local food systems. The findings will inform the design, implementation and scaling of programmes with potential to advance multiple SDGs.

## Ethics and dissemination

Ethical approval is not required as this systematic review analyses the existing literature, with no primary data collection or access to individual-level data. Findings will be disseminated via open-access publication, conferences and policy briefs to relevant international agencies and LMIC ministries, alongside a plain-language summary and PRISMA flow diagram on Open Sceince Framework (OSF) (https://osf.io/p83tb/), where search strategies, eligibility decisions and extraction tables will also be shared; all protocol amendments will be documented and dated on OSF.
